history.heading: Nomads of the desert
paragraphs: Western Sahara, on the northwest coast of Africa, is a sparsely populated desert territory. It has long been home to nomadic Sahrawi peoples of Arab and Amazigh (Berber) origin who spoke Hassaniya Arabic and herded camels and goats.
Spain claimed the coast in 1884 and established the colony of Spanish Sahara, which it fully controlled from the 1930s. Large phosphate deposits were discovered at Bou Craa in the 1940s.

history.heading: A disputed territory
paragraphs: As Spain prepared to leave, both Morocco and Mauritania claimed the territory. In 1975 the International Court of Justice found ties of allegiance with Morocco but no territorial sovereignty and supported self-determination. Morocco organised the Green March, in which about 350,000 Moroccans crossed into the territory. Spain withdrew in 1976.

The Polisario Front, a Sahrawi independence movement, proclaimed the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic (SADR) in 1976 and fought Morocco and Mauritania. Mauritania withdrew in 1979. Morocco built a 2,700 km sand wall (the Berm) and controls about 80 percent of the territory. A UN-brokered ceasefire in 1991 promised a referendum on independence, which has never taken place. The ceasefire broke down in 2020.

culture.heading: Sahrawi culture
paragraphs: Sahrawis speak Hassaniya Arabic and are Sunni Muslims. Traditional culture includes poetry, music with the tidinit lute, tea ceremonies and nomadic tents (khaima). Tens of thousands of Sahrawi refugees have lived for decades in camps near Tindouf, Algeria.

politics.heading: Contested status
paragraphs: Western Sahara is listed by the UN as a non-self-governing territory. Morocco administers most of it as its southern provinces and proposes autonomy under Moroccan sovereignty, a plan supported by the United States, France, Spain, the UK and others; in 2025 the UN Security Council endorsed it as a basis for negotiations. The Polisario, backed by Algeria, seeks a referendum on independence. The SADR is a member of the African Union and recognised by several dozen countries.

economy.heading: Phosphates and fishing
paragraphs: The economy is based on phosphate mining, rich coastal fishing grounds and Moroccan public investment in cities such as Laayoune and Dakhla, which have also developed renewable energy and tourism. Exploitation of the territory's resources is contested in international courts. The Moroccan dirham is used in Moroccan-controlled areas.
